<reason>Both sides argued competently, but B built the tighter, more mechanism-driven case and used the Pressure Questions round more decisively. B's Q2 forced A to finally quantify "meaningful share" (one quarter of marquee fixtures), and B immediately converted that concession—paired with A's own earlier admission in [A2.7] that "the rest of the schedule" could go to streamers—into a recurring "tell": the carve-out targets precisely the highest-exclusivity-premium inventory. A never fully neutralized this, instead retreating to "additional exclusivity premium, not core funding," which reads as assertion rather than rebuttal. A's honest concession in A4.1 that there is "no dollar-for-dollar replacement" further undercut its own revenue-neutrality claims without offering a real mechanism, which B repeatedly and correctly flagged ("hope is not a funding model"). A's strongest surviving thread was the access/barrier asymmetry (free terrestrial reception vs. recurring subscription cost), which B never fully closed, only reasserted "neither side is truly free." That kept A's case alive but not dominant. B's closing framing—"a guaranteed, quantified cost against an unguaranteed, already-substitutable benefit"—crystallized the clash more cleanly than A's closing, which mostly restated prior claims without resolving the mechanism gap B had exposed.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Pressure Question forcing A to define "meaningful share," followed by B's exploitation of A's own [A2.7] concession to reframe the carve-out as targeting the highest-value, highest-premium fixtures—a point A never squarely rebutted.</best_rebuttal>
